note: ARES Phase 3 science records. kind 'observation' = reported as seen or measured by Curiosity; 'published-interpretation' = explanation proposed by scientists in the cited source, not confirmed fact. The 'criteria' fields are ARES planning labels used by the prioritization method (documented in Stage 3.6); they are not NASA rankings. No target here has verified coordinates.

targets.name: Boxwork ridges
targets.short: Low, crisscrossing ridges that Curiosity first examined up close in 2025.
targets.relevance: Direct focus of the ARES mission question about past groundwater.

facts.text: Low ridges form crisscrossing patterns that stretch for miles across one layer of Mount Sharp.
Boxwork patterns have not been spotted elsewhere on the mountain by Curiosity or by orbiters.
Dark lines seen from orbit along the ridges were found, up close, to be fractures.
A drilled ridge sample contained clay minerals.
Scientists propose that groundwater flowed through fractures and left minerals that hardened the rock, and that wind later removed the softer rock around it.

targets.observedNote: Close-up views from 15 to 18 May 2025 (JPL, 2025). Panorama PIA26693 taken 26 Sept 2025.
limits: No published map coordinates in the sources ARES has checked.
Ridge height differs between sources: some just a few inches (JPL, June 2025) versus roughly 1 to 2 m (NASA, Feb 2026).
Sources are NASA news articles and image pages, not peer-reviewed papers.
Ridges are not shown to be walkable or safe for an astronaut.

targets.name: Sandy hollows between ridges
targets.short: Sandy low ground between ridges, with bedrock that differs from other Mount Sharp layers.
targets.relevance: Comparing hollow rock with ridge rock helps test how groundwater shaped each.

facts.text: A drilled bedrock sample from a hollow contained carbonate minerals.
Bedrock between ridges has a different composition from other layers of Mount Sharp.
Rover engineers noted wheel slipping and turning trouble in the sand of the hollows.

targets.observedNote: Sampling reported in NASA's Feb 2026 article; exact sample date not given in the sources checked.
limits: No published map coordinates in the sources ARES has checked.
The wheel-slip remark is a rover observation and does not establish anything about an astronaut on foot.
The sources do not name the hollow drill site.

targets.name: Nodule field
targets.short: Pea-sized bumps found on ridge walls and in hollows, imaged close-up on 21 Aug 2025.
targets.relevance: Nodules record minerals left as groundwater dried out, linking the boxwork to water history.

facts.text: Nodules were found along ridge walls and in the hollows between ridges, not near the central fractures.
The mosaic PIA26697 was taken with MAHLI on 21 Aug 2025 (sol 4636).
NASA says nodules like these were made by minerals left behind as water dried billions of years ago.
A mission scientist says the team cannot yet explain why the nodules sit where they do.

limits: NASA does not state where on the map the image was taken.
Why the nodules are located where they are remains an open question.

targets.name: Calcium sulfate veins
targets.short: White mineral-filled fractures in the bedrock between boxwork ridges.
targets.relevance: Veins are left by groundwater moving through rock cracks, directly tied to the mission question.

facts.text: The bedrock between ridges has many tiny fractures filled with white calcium sulfate veins.
Similar veins were common in lower layers of Mount Sharp but had not been seen in the sulfate layer until this region.
NASA identifies the wavy ridges between nodule groups in PIA26697 as calcium sulfate veins.
The veins were left behind as groundwater trickled through rock cracks.

targets.observedNote: Reported June 2025 (JPL); also visible in PIA26697 (21 Aug 2025).
targets.instrument: Not specified in the sources checked
limits: No published map coordinates in the sources ARES has checked.
The team has not yet explained why the veins returned in this layer (JPL, June 2025).

targets.name: Sulfate-bearing layer of Mount Sharp
targets.short: The salty-mineral layer of Mount Sharp that contains the boxwork region.
targets.relevance: Gives the geological setting: the boxwork formed in a layer that records drying climate.

facts.text: The layer Curiosity was exploring is rich in magnesium sulfates, salty minerals that form as water dries up.
The whole boxwork region is part of a layer on Mount Sharp enriched in sulfates.
Sulfates in this layer suggest it formed as the climate became drier, yet boxwork shows water still existed underground.

targets.observedNote: Not tied to a single observation date.
targets.instrument: Not specified in the sources checked
limits: A layer covers a large area and has no single coordinate; ARES does not give it a point marker.
Layer boundaries are not defined in the sources ARES has checked.

targets.name: Gould Mesa (butte)
targets.short: A distant butte whose cliff band and dark ridges may be early signs of boxwork.
targets.relevance: A possible nearby comparison area for boxwork-related terrain.

facts.text: Curiosity's Mastcam imaged the butte nicknamed Gould Mesa on 9 March 2025 (sol 4476).
A band of cliffs and dark ridges near the top of the butte may be the first glimpses of boxwork formations.

limits: NASA says the features 'may be' boxwork; this is not a confirmed identification.
Distance and location of the butte are not given in the source.
'Gould Mesa' is a mission nickname, not an official IAU name.

targets.name: Altadena drill sample
targets.short: A rock nicknamed Altadena, drilled on 8 June 2025 to study the bedrock's composition.
targets.relevance: A sample from the new region could help explain the bedrock's different composition.

facts.text: Curiosity drilled a rock nicknamed Altadena on 8 June 2025 and dropped the powder into instruments for analysis.

limits: The sources ARES has checked do not report Altadena's analysis results.
The sources do not say whether Altadena is the ridgetop, hollow or transitional sample.
No associated image has been verified.
targets.status: Sampled; results not checked by ARES
